lessons.title: Sockets: socket, bind, listen, accept, connect
lessons.goal:
Write a tiny TCP server and client, watch the system calls they make, and inspect the sockets with `ss`.

Why it matters: every network service is a process holding sockets. `ss` shows who listens, who is connected and how long the queues are, which is the first step in nearly every network incident.

setup.note: Programs are small C files. tcpdump and nc are used (`dnf install tcpdump nmap-ncat`). Everything runs on the loopback interface (127.0.0.1), so no traffic leaves this machine.

steps.title: A socket is a file descriptor for communication
steps.text: `socket()` creates an endpoint and returns a **file descriptor**. A server then calls `bind` (claim an address and port), `listen` (start accepting; the **backlog** is the length of the queue of waiting connections) and `accept` (take one connection, which gives a **new** descriptor). A client calls `connect`.

steps.title: The client program
steps.text: The client connects, sends `ping`, prints the answer.

steps.title: Run both under strace
steps.text: We start the server under `strace` (only the network calls) in the background, then run the client.

run.cmd: strace -f -o srv.trace -e trace=socket,bind,listen,accept,accept4,connect ./tcp_server > srv.out & sleep 2; ./tcp_client; wait; cat srv.out
run.output:
[1] 3479919
client got: pong
server got: ping

run.cmd: grep -E 'socket|bind|listen|accept' srv.trace | sed -E 's/^[0-9]+ +//; s/sa_data="[^"]*"/.../; s/inet_addr\("127.0.0.1"\)/127.0.0.1/' | cut -c1-100
run.output:
socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, IPPROTO_IP) = 3
bind(3, {sa_family=AF_INET, sin_port=htons(9000), sin_addr=127.0.0.1}, 16) = 0
listen(3, 5)                    = 0
accept(3, NULL, NULL)           = 4

steps.title: ss: who is listening?
steps.text: `ss` lists sockets. `-l` listening, `-t` TCP, `-n` numbers instead of names, `-p` the owning process. For a **listening** socket `Recv-Q` is the number of connections waiting to be accepted and `Send-Q` is the backlog limit.

run.output:
[1] 3479932
State Recv-Q Send-Q Local Peer
LISTEN 0 5 127.0.0.1:9000 users:(("tcp_server",pid=N,fd=N))

steps.title: ss: connected sockets and states
steps.text: After a client connects, the server has an established socket. `ss -tan` shows the state of every TCP socket: `LISTEN`, `ESTAB`, `TIME-WAIT`, ... Here the client connects and the server answers.

run.cmd: ./tcp_client; sleep 0.5; ss -tan 'sport = :9000 or dport = :9000' | awk '{print $1, $4, $5}' | sed -E 's/127.0.0.1:[0-9]{5}/127.0.0.1:EPHEMERAL/g'
run.output:
client got: pong
State Local Address:Port
TIME-WAIT 127.0.0.1:9000 127.0.0.1:EPHEMERAL
TIME-WAIT 127.0.0.1:EPHEMERAL 127.0.0.1:9000

steps.under: Each socket is a kernel `struct sock` reachable through a file descriptor (`ls -l /proc/PID/fd` shows `socket:[inode]`). For TCP the kernel keeps a state machine, send and receive buffers, retransmission timers and a congestion window per connection. Your program only sees `read` and `write` on the descriptor.

steps.title: The descriptor view
steps.text: A socket is listed like any open file.

run.cmd: ./tcp_server > /dev/null & p=$!; sleep 0.5; ls -l /proc/$p/fd | awk '/socket/ {print $9, $10, $11}' | sed -E 's#/proc/[0-9]+/fd/##; s/\[[0-9]+\]/[inode]/'; kill $p 2>/dev/null; wait $p 2>/dev/null; true

quiz.q: Which call turns a listening socket into a connected one for a client?
quiz.explain: `accept` returns a new descriptor for the connection.

quiz.q: For a listening socket in `ss -ltn`, what is Send-Q?
quiz.explain: Recv-Q is the current queue; Send-Q is its limit.

options: The process that owns each socket

quiz.q: What is the file descriptor of a socket in /proc/PID/fd shown as?

check.scenario: A service's port 8080 is not reachable, and you are logged in on the server. Which two commands tell you whether it is listening and on which address?
check.answer: `ss -ltnp | grep :8080` shows if a process listens and on **which address**: `127.0.0.1:8080` means local only, `0.0.0.0:8080` or `*:8080` means all interfaces. Then test locally with `curl -sv http://127.0.0.1:8080/` before suspecting the firewall.

lessons.title: The TCP handshake, states and queues
lessons.goal:
Watch the three-way handshake and the connection teardown in real packets, and connect the TCP states you see in `ss` with what happened on the wire.

Why it matters: `TIME_WAIT` piles, `CLOSE_WAIT` leaks and full accept queues are classic production problems. Each one is a state or a queue you can read.

setup.note: Programs are small C files. tcpdump and nc are used (`dnf install tcpdump nmap-ncat`). Everything runs on the loopback interface (127.0.0.1), so no traffic leaves this machine.

steps.title: Capture a connection on loopback
steps.text: `tcpdump -i lo` captures packets on the loopback interface. `nc -l` listens, a second `nc` connects, sends a line and closes. We print each packet as: source > destination [flags] length.

run.cmd: sudo timeout 4 tcpdump -i lo -nn -l 'tcp port 9001' 2>/dev/null | sed -E 's/^[0-9:.]+ IP ([^ ]+) > ([^:]+): Flags \[([^]]+)\].*length ([0-9]+)/\1 > \2 [\3] len=\4/' | sed -E 's/127.0.0.1\.[0-9]{5}/CLIENT/g' > cap.txt & T=$!; sleep 1; (nc -l 127.0.0.1 9001 > /dev/null &); sleep 0.5; echo hello | nc 127.0.0.1 9001; wait $T; cat cap.txt

steps.after: Read the flags: `S` SYN, `S.` SYN+ACK, `.` ACK, `P.` PUSH+ACK (data), `F.` FIN+ACK. The first three packets are the **three-way handshake**. The `P.` packet carries the 6 bytes of `hello\n`. The `F.` packets close each direction.

steps.title: What the handshake does
steps.text:
1. Client sends **SYN** with its initial sequence number and options (window size, MSS, timestamps).
2. Server answers **SYN+ACK**: it acknowledges the client's number and sends its own.
3. Client sends **ACK**. Both ends are now `ESTABLISHED`.

After the first SYN the server keeps the half-open connection in the **SYN queue**; after the ACK it moves to the **accept queue** until the program calls `accept`. If either queue is full the kernel drops packets and the client retries (seconds of delay).

steps.title: TIME-WAIT: the side that closes first waits
steps.text: The end that closes first ends in `TIME-WAIT` for about 60 seconds, to make sure the last ACK arrives and old packets die out. Many short connections therefore create many `TIME-WAIT` sockets on the **closing** side (that is normal).

run.cmd: ss -tan 'sport = :9001 or dport = :9001' | awk 'NR>1 {print $1}' | sort | uniq -c | awk '{print $2, $1}'

steps.under: TIME-WAIT lasts 2 x MSL (60 s on Linux, fixed in the kernel). `tcp_fin_timeout` is the time a socket stays in FIN-WAIT-2 for orphaned connections, not TIME-WAIT. Running out of ephemeral ports is solved by connection reuse (keep-alive, connection pools), not by shortening TIME-WAIT.

steps.title: CLOSE-WAIT: the other side forgot to close
steps.text: When the peer closes, our side gets a FIN and enters `CLOSE-WAIT`, waiting for **our application** to call `close()`. A growing number of `CLOSE-WAIT` sockets is an **application bug** (a connection leak), not a network problem. We create one: the server accepts and never closes; the client connects and closes.

run.cmd: python3 -c "import socket,time; s=socket.socket(); s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET,socket.SO_REUSEADDR,1); s.bind(('127.0.0.1',9002)); s.listen(); c,_=s.accept(); time.sleep(6)" & sleep 0.7; python3 -c "import socket; socket.create_connection(('127.0.0.1',9002)).close()"; sleep 0.5; ss -tan 'sport = :9002 or dport = :9002' | awk 'NR>1 {print $1}' | sort | tr '\n' ' '; echo; wait

steps.title: Summary of states
steps.text: `LISTEN` waiting for connections. `SYN-SENT` / `SYN-RECV` handshake in progress. `ESTAB` connected. `FIN-WAIT-1/2` we closed, waiting for the peer. `CLOSE-WAIT` peer closed, we have not. `LAST-ACK` we closed after the peer. `TIME-WAIT` waiting before the port can be reused.

run.cmd: ss -s | grep -E '^TCP:' | sed -E 's/[0-9]+ \(estab [0-9]+, closed [0-9]+, orphaned [0-9]+, timewait [0-9]+\)/(counts vary)/'

quiz.q: Which flags make up the three-way handshake?
Which state means the peer has closed but the local program has not?
quiz.explain: CLOSE-WAIT: a leak in the local application.

quiz.q: Which side normally ends up in TIME-WAIT?
options: The side that receives the FIN

quiz.q: What happens when the accept queue is full?
options: New connections are delayed or dropped; clients retry
quiz.explain: Packets are dropped and the client retransmits the SYN/ACK.

check.scenario: A web server shows 30 000 sockets in TIME-WAIT and users see errors `cannot assign requested address` when the app calls an upstream. What is happening and what do you do?
check.answer: The app opens many short connections to one upstream address, so the pool of ephemeral ports (`net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range`) is used up by TIME-WAIT sockets of the closing side. Fix by reusing connections (HTTP keep-alive, connection pooling), spreading across several upstream IPs or source IPs, or widening the port range. `tcp_tw_reuse=1` can help for outgoing connections.

interview.q: What system calls does a TCP server make?
interview.a: `socket`, `bind`, `listen`, then `accept` for each connection (which returns a new descriptor), `read`/`write`, `close`. A client uses `socket`, `connect`. See [the lesson](#/lesson/29/sockets-and-ss).

interview.q: How do you list listening ports and their processes?
interview.a: `ss -ltnp` (add `-u` for UDP). The local address tells if it listens on all interfaces or only on loopback.
SYN from the client, SYN+ACK from the server, ACK from the client. Then the connection is ESTABLISHED. See [the lesson](#/lesson/29/tcp-handshake-states).

interview.q: What does a growing number of CLOSE_WAIT sockets mean?
interview.a: The peer closed the connections and the local application is not calling close(): a connection leak in the application.
So the closing side can resend the final ACK and so late packets of the old connection cannot be mistaken for a new one on the same ports. It lasts 60 s on Linux.

interview.q: What do Recv-Q and Send-Q mean for a listening socket?
interview.a: Recv-Q: connections currently waiting in the accept queue. Send-Q: the maximum backlog (min of listen() backlog and net.core.somaxconn).

glossary.def: A kernel endpoint for communication, used through a file descriptor.
The queue length of connections waiting to be accepted on a listening socket.
SYN, SYN+ACK, ACK: how a TCP connection is set up.
TCP state of the side that closed first, kept ~60 s before the ports can be reused.
TCP state: the peer closed, the local application has not yet.
A temporary source port the kernel picks for an outgoing connection.
